progress.subscribe-failed: Could not subscribe to status updates.

action.apply-tooltip-clean: Everything on screen is already applied.
action.apply-tooltip-pending: Send the changes on screen to the background service.
action.apply-tooltip-service-stopped: The rules on screen are not applied to the service. It is stopped, so Apply saves them to your rules file for now and stays available until the service can take them.
action.revoke-admin-tooltip: End the temporary administrator approval granted this session. The next change will ask for approval again.
action.minimize-to-tray: Minimize to tray instead of close

service.title: Service management
service.description: NetRuleRouter runs as a Windows background service. Install or manage it from here. Administrator rights (a UAC prompt) are required for install / uninstall / start / stop.
service.admin-hint: These actions require administrator approval — asked once per session.

status.transition-hint: This is normal and usually takes a few seconds — no action needed.

reason.not-registered: Service is not registered in the system.

action.stop-tooltip: Stops the background service. By default all routes are removed and every connection returns to your main connection; leak-protection blocks are always removed. (Turn on "Keep matched routes on the additional adapter" in Settings to keep your routed sites on the additional adapter — e.g. a work/corporate adapter.) Note: simply closing the app keeps routing active, because the service keeps running.

service.auto-start-help: Service starts automatically on system boot when enabled.

start-mode.heading: When the service starts
start-mode.help: “Start with Windows” keeps your rules enforced from boot, before anyone logs in (best for always-on or managed setups). “Start when the app opens” runs the service only while you use NetRuleRouter and lets the app start it without an administrator prompt every time. Changing this needs administrator approval.

launch-tray.label: Also start the tray at sign-in
launch-tray.description: The service starts at boot before anyone logs in and cannot open the tray itself. This starts the tray icon when you sign in — the same setting as “Start the tray automatically at sign-in” in General.

service.crash-recovery: Service will auto-restart up to 3 times after failures.

admin-auto-revoke.title: Administrator rights
admin-auto-revoke.disable-label: Do not revoke administrator approval automatically
admin-auto-revoke.note: After you approve administrator access, it stays available without new prompts. If it sits unused for this long, the app gives it up on its own; the next administrative action will ask again.

console.title: Command-line console
console.description: NetRuleRouter ships a small console for service tasks: install, start, stop and check the service. Add its folder to your PATH to run it as "nrr-cli" from any terminal.
console.path-registered: The console can be run from any terminal.
console.path-not-registered: The console can only be run from its own folder — and in PowerShell you still have to spell it ".\nrr-cli.exe", because a bare name is not searched for in the current directory.
console.add-to-path-tooltip: Adds the console's folder to your personal PATH. It affects your account only, needs no administrator rights, and changes nothing else on the list.
console.path-added: The console was added to your PATH.
console.path-already-present: The console was already on your PATH.
console.path-failed: Could not add the console to your PATH.
console.new-terminal-hint: Terminals that are already open keep the PATH they started with. Open a new one, or run this line in the current one:

presets.title: Presets and settings
presets.description: Import or export rules in plain-text format. Each route has its own preset file; the other route's rules are carried over from the active revision on import.
presets.full-settings-description: Export adapter bindings, behavior mode, and rules-file paths as a single YAML file. Useful for backing up or transferring your settings.

bundled-presets.title: Bundled presets
bundled-presets.label: Show the bundled-preset quick-load row in Rules
bundled-presets.description: Shows a quick-load dropdown of bundled country/demo presets above the rules table. The "Hide" button on that row also turns this off.

user-folder.title: My rule sets
user-folder.description: Point the quick-load dropdown at your own folder instead of the sets that come with the app. The folder can hold "rules_primary.txt" and "rules_secondary.txt" directly, or one subfolder per set — each subfolder's name becomes the entry in the dropdown.
user-folder.placeholder: Using the rule sets that come with the app
user-folder.dialog-title: Choose the folder with your rule sets
user-folder.use-bundled-path: Point at the sets that come with the app

save-as-set.button: Save current rules as a set...
save-as-set.needs-folder: Choose a folder above first — that is where a new set is saved.
save-as-set.title: Save rules as a set
save-as-set.prompt: The current rules of both routes are saved as a new set in your folder. Name it so you can tell it apart later, for example "work" or "home".
save-as-set.name-invalid: A name cannot contain \ / : or ".." — it is a folder name, not a path.

bundled-write-warning.title: This folder belongs to the app
bundled-write-warning.body: You are saving into the folder the app keeps its own rule sets in. Updating the app replaces that folder, and your set is lost with it. Pick a folder of your own above to keep sets safely.
bundled-write-warning.dont-ask: I understand — do not ask again

note.logs-diagnostics: Preview controls are available on dedicated screens.
note.experimental: This section is reserved for upcoming experimental options.
note.route-labels: You can rename the two routes for the UI without changing routing behavior.
note.presets: When enabled, selecting a preset for one route automatically opens a file picker for the other route.

allow-mode-a.label: Allow kill-switch mode A (legacy)
allow-mode-a.note: Mode A is a legacy enforcement mode kept only for historical reference. It is not maintained, may not work, and can be removed in a future release. Mode B (the local DNS resolver) is the supported mechanism. Turn this on only if you specifically need to pick mode A in the routing settings.

detailed-mode.label: Detailed mode
detailed-mode.note: Shows the fine-grained fake-IP switches (UDP relay, instant reset) under Settings → Routing. Off by default: without it, NetRuleRouter uses sensible defaults for them. The main routing switches stay visible either way.

pre-flight-apply-policy.label: Offer the pre-flight apply-check policy
pre-flight-apply-policy.note: Adds "Pre-flight, then all-or-nothing" to the apply failure policy in Settings → Routing. The pre-flight checks themselves are still in development — until they land, this option behaves the same as All or nothing.

isp-block-candidates.label: Suggest a rule when a site is blocked by your provider
isp-block-candidates.note: When a site will not open because your internet provider is blocking it, NetRuleRouter offers to move that site to your additional route instead of leaving it unreachable.

field.notify-suggestion-changes: Tell me when the suggested-addresses list changes
field.notify-block-notices: Tell me when a connection gets blocked
field.hide-block-notice-addresses-tooltip: Replaces the destination with a generic label instead of the real hostname — useful when your screen is being shared or recorded.
field.auto-confirm-adapter-id: Auto-confirm a reinstalled additional adapter when its name matches
field.auto-confirm-adapter-id-tooltip: When an additional adapter is reinstalled and gets a new ID, re-bind it automatically if the saved name uniquely matches a live adapter. Turn off to confirm each change manually via the banner.
field.block-secondary-traffic: Block connections when secondary is unavailable
field.rules-file-change-mode: When rules file changes on disk
field.show-other-os-rules: Show rules for other operating systems

zone-ip-priority.label: Zone vs. IP priority
zone-ip-priority.description: When a Zone rule and an Exact IP rule both match the same destination, choose which takes priority.

failure-policy.title: Apply failure policy
failure-policy.description: Choose how the service handles partial failures during multi-step rule application.

best-effort.label: Best effort (recommended)
best-effort.description: Rules that can't be enforced on this host (app not installed, host not yet resolved, missing adapter) are skipped and reported; the rest are applied. Default.

all-or-nothing.label: All or nothing
all-or-nothing.description: If any single rule can't be enforced, the whole apply rolls back. Exact-or-nothing.

pre-flight.label: Pre-flight, then all-or-nothing (experimental)
pre-flight.description: Run predictable-failure checks before applying. Apply still rolls back on real errors. The checks themselves are still in development — this behaves the same as All or nothing today.
pre-flight.description-stale: Selected, but the Experimental opt-in for this option is off. The checks are still in development — this behaves the same as All or nothing today.

failure-policy.requires-elevation: Changing this setting requires administrator elevation.

pause.title: Apply rules
pause.persistence-hint: Disabling stops applying rules until you re-enable them. Setting persists across restarts.
pause.no-tray-warning: Tray is not running. Rules apply only while the tray is active.

default-route.title: Default route for unmatched traffic
default-route.description: Where traffic that matches no rule is sent. Rules always take priority. Default: primary route.

enforcement-mode.label: How routed traffic is enforced
enforcement-mode.option-resolver: Local DNS resolver (Mode B) — enforce before connect
enforcement-mode.note: Mode B sends system DNS through a local resolver so a routed site is enforced before its first packet — closing the leak window Mode A can't. It is invasive (redirects DNS) and IPv4-only; leave it off unless you are testing it. Changing this applies immediately — no service restart needed.

dns-via-secondary.label: DNS through the tunnel
dns-via-secondary.note: Site names are looked up through the additional connection instead of your provider's resolver, so the provider can neither see nor alter the answers. Some providers return a wrong or empty address for certain sites, which makes those sites fail to load even when routing is correct. If the additional connection is not available, lookups fall back to the main one. Off by default.

dns-fast-answers.label: Fast DNS answers
dns-fast-answers.note: Answer apps immediately; route protection finishes in the background. Turning this off can slow down page loads.

fake-ip.label: Route sites over virtual addresses (fake-IP)
fake-ip.note: Each routed site is answered with its own virtual address, so routing stays per-site even when several sites share one real server address — and protection no longer races the first connection. Requires Mode B (local DNS resolver). On Windows, turning this on loads the bundled Wintun virtual-adapter driver (signed by WireGuard LLC). Off by default.

fake-ip-udp-relay.label: Fake-IP UDP relay (experimental)
fake-ip-udp-relay.note: Carry QUIC/HTTP-3 through the relay instead of forcing browsers to fall back to TCP.

fake-ip-instant-rst.label: Instant reset when the additional route is unavailable
fake-ip-instant-rst.note: On (default): apps get an immediate connection reset when the additional route can't be resolved, so they can retry or fail over right away. Off: connections are held for up to 10 seconds while the route comes back, instead of resetting immediately.

mode-a-coverage.label: When the additional route is unavailable (Mode A)
mode-a-coverage.option-per-ip: Block only the learned addresses of routed sites (may briefly leak)
mode-a-coverage.note: Applies while leak protection is armed and the additional adapter is down or unresolved. “Block all unresolved traffic” closes the gap where a routed site rotates to a fresh, not-yet-learned IP that would otherwise leak over the primary link. VPN clients and apps routed to the primary adapter stay exempt so the tunnel can always reconnect.

hosts-bypass.label: Resolve routed domains bypassing the hosts file
hosts-bypass.note: On (default): routed domains are resolved directly against your DNS server, so a local hosts/adblock entry pinning a routed site to 127.0.0.1 cannot silently disable its routing. Turn off only if you rely on hosts-file overrides for the sites you route.

auto-rules.title: Auto-rules
auto-rules.label: Missing companion domains
auto-rules.note: A routed site often loads its images and video from other domains your rules do not list, so the page opens but its content does not. By default NetRuleRouter collects these missing domains and offers them in the tray — nothing is added to your rules without your confirmation. “Apply automatically” adds them for you; “Off” stops collecting them altogether.
auto-rules.auto-save-note: Added addresses are written straight into the rules files your routes are linked to.
auto-rules.eager-label: Offer content-delivery domains without waiting for analysis
auto-rules.eager-note: Off by default. Content-delivery domains are usually named alike, so this makes media load sooner. Advertising and tracking networks are named alike too, so some of what appears will not be worth routing — review before you accept it.

doh-lockdown.title: Block browser DoH/DoT
doh-lockdown.label: Block browser DoH/DoT
doh-lockdown.note: Off by default. Browsers that resolve names over DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH) or DNS-over-TLS (DoT) hide their queries, so routed sites resolved that way bypass leak protection. Turning this on blocks known encrypted-DNS endpoints so name resolution falls back to plaintext DNS that NetRuleRouter can observe.
doh-lockdown.scope-leak-protection-only: Only while leak protection is active (recommended)
doh-lockdown.scope-leak-protection-only-note: Blocks encrypted DNS only while a block-all leak guard is armed, where DoH would otherwise defeat observation. Leaves DoH working the rest of the time. Recommended.
doh-lockdown.scope-always-note: Blocks encrypted DNS at all times, even when leak protection is off — maximum observability, but it breaks DoH/HTTP-3 for every app and can slow name resolution.
doh-lockdown.details: Blocking works by denying connections to a known list of DoH/DoT resolver endpoints (edited below). Apps then fall back to the operating system's plaintext DNS, which the observer reads to keep routing and leak protection accurate. Some apps pin their own resolver and may show connection errors until DoH is turned off in their own settings; this does not affect apps that use the system resolver.

resolvers.requires-admin: This is a shared, machine-wide list. Saving changes requires administrator approval.
resolvers.description: Endpoints blocked when the lockdown is active. Add a public resolver by IP address or hostname; untick a row to keep it in the list but stop blocking it.
resolvers.save-failed: Could not save the resolver list:
resolvers.load-failed: Could not load the resolver list:
resolvers.uac-declined: Administrator approval was declined; the resolver list was not saved.

hosts-file.label: OS hosts file
hosts-file.note: The OS hosts file can redirect or block a hostname before NetRuleRouter sees it (ad-block lists often map hosts to 127.0.0.1). NetRuleRouter never edits it — open the folder to inspect or edit it yourself (requires administrator).

liveness-window.label: Secondary tunnel liveness window
liveness-window.note: Optional. When set, NetRuleRouter actively pings the additional adapter's next hop; if it stays unreachable for this many seconds, leak protection fail-closes even if no traffic has failed yet. Off by default. It may false-positive if the tunnel peer silently drops ICMP (many VPNs do), so leave it off unless you know the peer answers pings.

rule-lock.heading: Who can change the rules

allow.label: Allow users to change routing rules
allow.tooltip: On (default): anyone signed in to this computer can add, edit and apply their own routing rules. Turn it off on company laptops, or for parental control, so only an administrator decides where traffic goes.

rule-lock.help: Affects the whole machine and needs administrator approval. While it is off, the Rules view is read-only for everyone: viewing, searching and exporting still work, but adding, editing, applying, importing and resetting to the baseline are turned off. The background service refuses the change as well, so the lock does not depend on this window.

vpn-client.title: Your VPN client
vpn-client.note: Point NetRuleRouter at the program you use as your VPN so its traffic keeps flowing over your main link while leak protection is on.

shared-addresses.title: Shared addresses (one IP serving several sites)
shared-addresses.routing-axis: While the secondary adapter is up: whether a shared IP is routed through it.
shared-addresses.blocking-axis: While the secondary adapter is down: whether shared addresses are blocked.

kill-switch.title: Leak protection
kill-switch.enable-label: Enable kill switch / leak protection (block traffic when the additional adapter is down)
kill-switch.enable-note: Off by default. While off, nothing is blocked — if the additional adapter drops, traffic falls back to your main link (this can expose your real address, which is fine if you don't need blocking). Turn it on to reveal the blocking options below.
kill-switch.always-on: While leak protection is ON and the additional adapter can't be reached — it is down, not started, or was reinstalled under a new name — traffic matched by your rules is blocked instead of leaking over your primary route. Choose what happens below.
kill-switch.label: Leak protection: if a site routed to the additional adapter is unavailable, block it instead of leaking over the primary route
kill-switch.summary: If the additional adapter drops, traffic matched by your rules is blocked instead of leaking over your primary route.
kill-switch.description: Closes the leak window with no race. Protection is armed automatically as soon as an additional adapter is assigned, and it stays armed whenever that adapter can't be found — it is down, was never started, or was reinstalled under a new name/ID (common with VPNs). In every one of those cases traffic that should use the adapter is blocked rather than sent over the primary route under your real address. What gets blocked depends on the routing behavior above: 'only selected' protects the matched destinations — the sites, IPs and applications you routed to the additional adapter; 'everything via the additional adapter' blocks all traffic except your local network, DHCP and the route exceptions. Traffic you did NOT route to the additional adapter keeps using your normal connection by design, so a ping to a random site you never routed is not blocked.
kill-switch.coverage-note: How coverage works: protection tracks the IP addresses a routed site resolves to, learned by watching your system's DNS. It extends automatically as new addresses appear (e.g. when a site behind a CDN rotates IPs), but a brand-new address has a brief unprotected moment until it is seen. Apps that resolve names themselves over DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH) bypass this — turn off DoH in the browser/app for full protection. A diagnostic ping is the hardest case: it fires a single packet the instant a name resolves — before protection can catch up — and pinging a bare IP address skips name-based routing entirely; neither reflects how apps normally connect.
kill-switch.block-all-label: When the additional adapter is unavailable, block ALL traffic (kill-switch), not just its routed sites
kill-switch.block-all-note: Most aggressive: while the additional adapter is down, only your local network and already-known primary sites keep working — everything else, including ping and new name (DNS) lookups, is blocked. This is what stops routed sites (and ICMP) from leaking to the primary link. Requires the leak-guard (fail-closed) to be on. While armed, the FIRST connection to a newly-seen allowed site can fail — its permit installs right after the name is first observed, so a refresh a second later goes through. Note: leak protection currently covers IPv4 only.
kill-switch.block-all-alert: Heads up: with this on, if the additional adapter (VPN) goes down your normal internet stops too — only your local network keeps working — until it comes back. Leave it off if you want your main connection to keep working when the VPN drops.
kill-switch.allow-dns-label: Allow name resolution over the main link while blocked (keep zones resolving)
kill-switch.allow-dns-note: On by default: a narrow exception (port 53 only) keeps name resolution working over your main link while blocked, so zones keep resolving — a deliberate, narrow DNS leak. Turn this off only for strict blocking: with DNS cut too, you have no working internet at all until the block clears. Useful with the local DNS resolver (Mode B) so zone rules keep working.
kill-switch.shared-strict-label: Strict: also block addresses shared with regular sites (may break them)
kill-switch.shared-strict-note: Off (smart, recommended): an address that a routed site shares with an ordinary site is not blocked, so the ordinary site keeps working — at the cost of the routed site's traffic to that shared address not being protected while the additional adapter is down. On (strict): every routed address is blocked, including shared ones — no leak, but co-hosted ordinary sites (for example google.com sharing addresses with routed Google services) stop opening while the block is active.
kill-switch.shared-smart-warning: Kill-switch strictness is reduced: shared addresses excluded from blocking —
kill-switch.shared-smart-list-unavailable: The running service reports how many addresses were excluded, but not which ones.
kill-switch.block-all-active-banner: Leak protection is blocking unknown traffic: the additional adapter can't be found (down, not started, or reinstalled under a new ID). Sites open as they become known; reconnect the VPN or re-bind the adapter to lift the block.
kill-switch.block-all-warn-label: Warn when leak protection blocks all unknown traffic
kill-switch.block-all-warn-note: On by default: a banner appears while the full block is active. Turn it off if you deliberately keep the service running with the VPN disconnected (e.g. from OS startup) and don't want the reminder.

failure-mode.label: If the additional adapter can't be found or is unavailable (offline)
failure-mode.desc-fail-closed: Safest: if NetRuleRouter can't find the additional adapter (it's down, or the binding is stale), matched traffic is blocked instead of leaking over the primary route. Leak protection always works.
failure-mode.desc-fail-open: Convenience: if the additional adapter can't be found, matched traffic keeps flowing over the primary route and a warning is shown. Your real address may be exposed.

protocols.label: Protocols leak protection cuts
protocols.desc: Which IP protocols leak protection drops. ICMP covers ping/traceroute. TCP/UDP are enforced at the connection layer; ICMP/IGMP/GRE/ESP at the packet layer. All on by default — uncheck to let a protocol through even while the block is active.
protocols.tcp-tooltip: Most web, email and app traffic (HTTP/HTTPS and similar).
protocols.udp-tooltip: DNS, video calls, games and other real-time traffic.
protocols.icmp-tooltip: Ping and traceroute. These live only at the packet layer, so ICMP must be checked for the block to stop a ping.
protocols.igmp-tooltip: Multicast group membership on the local network.
protocols.gre-tooltip: A tunnelling protocol used by some VPNs (e.g. PPTP).
protocols.other-tooltip: Legacy option: previously blocked every remaining IP protocol system-wide. The emergency block now cuts only the named protocols above; exotic protocols outside this list are not blocked.

level.label: Log detail level
level.description: Controls how much detail appears in the Logs screen and is written to the log store.
level.desc-info: Normal operation messages. Recommended for everyday use.
level.desc-warning: Warnings about recoverable conditions (stale cache, brief unavailability).
level.desc-debug: Detailed trace output — rule matching decisions and availability snapshots.
level.desc-critical: Critical errors only. Minimum log volume.

browser-stub.label: Browser stub on connection block
browser-stub.description: When Fail-Closed blocks a browser connection, show a built-in stub page instead of a silent connection error. Requires the process to be identified as a known browser.
browser-stub.experimental-warning: Experimental — behaviour may change without notice.

routing-behavior.ip-routing-note: Routing works by IP address. A website that checks and shows your IP (like 2ip.ru or whatismyipaddress.com) can still display your provider's address: its measurement endpoint often lives on a different IP than the page itself, or a single IP is shared by several sites. If you use a general-purpose VPN as the additional adapter, such a site can also keep showing your provider's IP and country when it is not one of your routed rules — that traffic goes over your primary link, while your routed sites still go through the VPN. This is a known limitation, not a routing failure. Per-site (per-hostname) steering on a shared IP is not supported yet.

include-subdomains.label: Also cover subdomains for domain rules (treat “example.com” as “example.com” + “*.example.com”)
include-subdomains.note: On by default: a rule for a site also covers that site's subdomains, so images and scripts from “cdn.example.com” take the same route as “example.com”. Applies to all your domain rules at once. It only catches subdomains of the SAME site — an IP-check served from a different provider (a third-party domain) still won't be covered — and it sends more traffic through the additional adapter. Turn it off to match the exact domain only.

shared-ip.label: When a routed domain shares an IP address with other sites
shared-ip.option-majority-of-ip: Route the shared IP only if most sites on it are yours (balanced)
shared-ip.option-majority-of-rules: Route the shared IP only if it holds most of your rules (cautious)
shared-ip.option-any-rule-domain: Always route the whole shared IP (aggressive)
shared-ip.note: Some sites (e.g. behind Cloudflare) share one IP with unrelated sites, and IP routing can't tell them apart. “Balanced” routes such an IP through the additional adapter only when your sites are the majority on it; “Cautious” only when that IP carries most of your rules; “Aggressive” always routes it (the others on it come along too). Truly separating two sites on one IP by name is not implemented in the current version.

prefer-primary.label: Selected sites only (via the additional adapter)
prefer-primary.description: Only the sites, IPs and apps in your rules use the additional adapter; all other traffic stays on your main connection. It routes by resolved IP address, so sites on shared CDNs or apps using DNS-over-HTTPS can occasionally slip onto your main connection. For a guarantee that nothing leaks, choose “Everything via the additional adapter — no leaks”.

prefer-secondary-when-available.label: Everything via the additional adapter
prefer-secondary-when-available.description: All traffic goes through the additional adapter while it is available. If it drops, traffic falls back to your main connection — your real address may be exposed until it reconnects.

strict-secondary-fail-closed.label: Everything via the additional adapter — no leaks
strict-secondary-fail-closed.description: All traffic goes through the additional adapter. If it drops, everything is blocked — nothing ever leaks over your main connection. This is the strongest no-leak guarantee (recommended when you use a VPN). Requires an additional adapter to be assigned.
strict-secondary-fail-closed.warning: If the additional adapter becomes unavailable, ALL traffic is blocked until it reconnects or you change this setting.

routing-behavior.default-mode-note: When no additional adapter is configured, your main connection is used by default.
routing-behavior.recommended-for-secondary-note: For a full guarantee that nothing leaks, choose “Everything via the additional adapter — no leaks”: all traffic goes through it and is blocked if it ever drops.

retention.title: Revisions retention
retention.description: Controls how long superseded, rejected, and rolled-back revisions are kept before pruning.
retention.pin-lkg-hint: The most recent superseded revision is pinned and excluded from age and count limits.

autosave.label: Save changes automatically after
autosave.help: Changes on this page are saved automatically once you stop editing, when you press Apply, and when you leave the page. Reset restores the factory defaults.

autostart.label: Start NetRuleRouter tray automatically at sign-in
autostart.description: Adds an entry under HKEY_CURRENT_USER\…\Run that launches the tray icon.

state.overridden: Registry value points to another binary — toggle to repair.

show-welcome.label: Show welcome wizard again...
show-welcome.description: Re-runs the first-launch flow: service install prompt (if not yet installed) and then the preset wizard. Useful when you want to import a different starter rule set.

autoload.title: Auto-load rules on startup
autoload.label: Load rules from the last-used files automatically at startup
autoload.description: When off, NetRuleRouter shows whatever the service already has and does not re-read the files on launch. The remembered file paths are kept.

merge-conflict.title: Merging file and app rules
merge-conflict.description: When you merge a linked rules file with the rules the app is already enforcing, this decides who wins for a rule that exists on both sides but differs. "Ask me" keeps both and lets you pick per rule; "File wins" / "Service wins" resolve automatically.

forget-binding.label: Forget file binding
forget-binding.description: Clears the remembered rules file paths. The next launch loads nothing from disk — you see exactly what the service has.

import-only-active.title: Importing presets
import-only-active.label: Import only active rules
import-only-active.description: When on, rules that are turned off in the imported preset (for example application rules, which can't route yet) are skipped instead of added as disabled rows. Turn off to import everything.

updates.not-implemented: This feature is not yet implemented and will be available in a future release.

compat-banner-mode.label: Compatibility banner
compat-banner-mode.description: Controls when the GUI shows the version-mismatch banner. "Automatic" only warns on an incompatible protocol.

traffic.title: Traffic statistics
traffic.description: How much traffic goes through the additional (VPN) adapter versus directly over the primary — received and sent per adapter.
traffic.period-today-note: All traffic accounted by the service today, with or without the additional adapter
traffic.period-session-note: Counted while the additional adapter session is active
traffic.session-none: The additional adapter has not come up yet — no session so far
traffic.no-data: No data yet — counting starts once traffic flows.
traffic.service-stopped: Statistics are not being collected while the service is stopped.
traffic.tunnel-overlap-note: While a VPN session is active, the primary row excludes traffic that transited into the tunnel.

storage.title: Storage usage
storage.description: On-disk footprint of the service state, cache, and log stores.

service-stability.title: Service stability
service-stability.help: These options only affect the control channel (IPC). Network policy enforcement runs independently.
service-stability.reset-tooltip: Reset to factory defaults (recoverable, 20 restarts, 100 ms, 5 s)

recoverable.label: Recoverable (recommended)
recoverable.help: If the GUI ↔ service control channel fails, the supervisor restarts it automatically. Policy enforcement keeps running. After all retry attempts are exhausted, the GUI marks the channel as unavailable but the service continues operating.

critical.label: Critical (fail-fast)
critical.help: Any control-channel failure puts the service into recovery mode. Policy enforcement halts until the operator restarts the service. Use for strict compliance scenarios.

ipc.cap-below-base: Max backoff must be greater than or equal to initial backoff.

verbose.label: Verbose service logging
verbose.tooltip: When enabled, the service writes tracing::debug events to operational NDJSON. Applies immediately, no restart required.
verbose.help: Useful for diagnosing rare IPC or mutation issues. Leave off in normal operation — log volume grows substantially.

conn-trace.heading: Connection trace (diagnostic)
conn-trace.intro: Records outgoing connections of all apps and the interface each left through (direct vs the additional adapter). Sees the real socket, so it works even when the browser uses DoH. Requires service restart.

ndjson.label: Write connection trace to service log (NDJSON)
ndjson.tooltip: Each observed connection is written to the operational NDJSON: process, remote IP:port, and egress interface (primary/provider or secondary/additional adapter).

gui.label: Show connection trace in diagnostics (GUI)
gui.tooltip: Surfaces the connection trace in the diagnostics log view (also writes it to NDJSON).

conn-trace.help: Privacy-sensitive: the trace contains per-connection process names and remote addresses. Leave off in normal operation.

rule-scope.heading: When routing rules are enforced

service-driven.label: Keep enforcing while the service runs (even when the app is closed)
service-driven.tooltip: On (default): the service enforces your rules continuously — from boot, even with no window or tray icon open — until the service is stopped. Best for always-on or managed/business setups. Off: rules apply only while the app or tray is running; fully exiting the app removes every added route and returns the network to normal.

rule-scope.help: Affects the whole machine and needs administrator approval. On = always-on (managed/business deployments). Off = active only while you keep the app open. Stopping the service always clears the routes.

routing-stop.heading: When routing is paused or the service stops

persist.label: Keep rule routes on the additional adapter after pause/stop (route persistence, not leak protection)
persist.tooltip: Default (off): full teardown — every route is removed and ALL traffic returns to your main connection; matched sites stop using the additional adapter. Turn ON to keep the matched routes on the additional adapter — useful for a work/corporate additional adapter, so you keep reaching corporate resources while general routing is paused; for a general-purpose additional adapter leave it off so everything returns to your main connection. NetRuleRouter's overlays are still removed either way. Leak-protection blocks are always removed on pause/stop, so a paused or stopped service can never lock you out.

routing-stop.help: Applies to both “safe disable”/pause and stopping the service. Affects the whole machine and needs administrator approval. Note: simply closing the app keeps routing active because the background service keeps running — use Stop service (or Disable) to turn routing off.

cache-refresh.heading: Address cache refresh
cache-refresh.label: Re-resolve routed sites every
cache-refresh.help: How often a routed site's IP addresses are refreshed (1 min – 24 h). Site IPs rarely change, so a longer interval means less network activity; the last known address is always kept and used for routing and leak-protection until a fresh one is obtained, so lengthening this never weakens blocking.

show-audit-tab.help: The security audit trail is always recorded, regardless of this setting. This only shows or hides the audit viewing tab in the Logs view.

status.rule-lock-off: Users can change the routing rules on this computer.

action.assign-unavailable-tooltip: Adapter is currently unavailable — the role will activate automatically when it comes back up.

external-ip.probe-failed: Could not determine the external address:

locked.banner-title: Rules are managed by your administrator

rules.preview-notice: Rule changes take effect only after you review and apply them.

state.in-sync: The rules match the service and your rules file.
state.not-applied-tooltip: The rules shown here differ from the ones the service is enforcing. Apply them.

state.unknown: Not verified — the service isn't reachable right now.

bundled-preset.label: Bundled preset:
bundled-preset.hide-tooltip: Hide the bundled-preset quick-load row. Re-enable it in Settings.
bundled-preset.folder-empty-hint: Your presets folder is empty — showing bundled sets

action.show-service-rules-tooltip: Load the rules the service is currently enforcing into the table.
action.reset-to-baseline-tooltip: Discard your custom rules and return to the baseline rules shared on this computer.
action.set-baseline-tooltip: Administrator: make the current rules the baseline that every user on this computer falls back to. Asks for administrator approval.
action.load-demo-rules-tooltip: Merge the bundled built-in demo rules into the table and open the review flow.

action.export-source-secondary: Export only the additional route's rules to a file...

action.select-row: Select this rule for bulk actions
action.delete-single-body: Rule {id} ({value}) will be removed from this app. Apply the change to the service later via 'Save and review...'.

bulk.delete-body: {n} selected rule(s) will be removed. You can apply the change to the service later via 'Save and review...'.

rules.application-routing-note: Routes everything this app connects to through the additional adapter. NetRuleRouter learns the app's destinations by watching its connections, so routing fills in as the app connects — enable «Connection observation» in Settings → Diagnostics for this to work. Enter the executable name, e.g. chrome.exe.

import-only-active.label: Import only active rules
import-only-active.tooltip: When loading a preset, skip rules that are turned off in it (for example application rules, which can't route yet). Default comes from Settings → General; changing it here applies to imports this session only.

hint.zone: A single zone label — letters, digits, hyphens; an optional leading dot is allowed. Matches all hosts in the zone. Examples: .ru, ru, com, intra, corp.
hint.domain: FQDN (example.com) or wildcard suffix (*.example.com). Matches the domain itself and all subdomains. Examples: example.com, *.example.com, mail.example.com.
hint.exact-ip: Exact IPv4 address. Each octet 0–255; first octet ≥ 1. Examples: 192.0.2.1, 8.8.8.8, 203.0.113.7.
hint.application-windows: Process filename — .exe, .ps1, .bat or any executable script. Exact (browser.exe) or glob (*vpn*.exe).
hint.application-macos: Process filename or app bundle id.

column.enabled-tooltip: Click to toggle all visible rules on/off.
column.select-tooltip: Select / deselect all visible rules for bulk actions.

preview.invalid-ip-comment: preview: invalid IP — surfaces the strict validator

search.placeholder: Search by match value or comment

source.label: Source:
source.open-folder-tooltip: Open the folder containing this rules file in Explorer.

hosts-override.tooltip: The operating system's hosts file resolves this hostname before NetRuleRouter sees any traffic, so NetRuleRouter cannot override it. Edit the OS hosts file to change this.

duplicate-dialog.title: Duplicate rule
duplicate-dialog.message: This rule exists in both the primary and secondary lists. Choose which list to keep it in.

match-value-invalid.zone: Zone is a single label — letters, digits, and hyphens only (no dots).
match-value-invalid.domain: Enter a domain name (example.com) or a subdomain wildcard (*.example.com).
match-value-invalid.domain-glob-position: Wildcard `*` is allowed only as a leading prefix (`*.example.com`).
match-value-invalid.exact-ip-octet-out-of-range: Octet {octet} (position {position}) is out of range. Each octet must be 0–255.
match-value-invalid.exact-ip-first-octet-zero: First octet must be ≥ 1 (0.x.x.x is reserved).
match-value-invalid.exact-ip-broadcast: 255.255.255.255 is the limited-broadcast address and cannot be routed.
match-value-invalid.application: Enter a process filename or glob (e.g. browser.exe, *vpn*.exe, script.ps1).

match-value-warning.exact-ip-loopback: Loopback addresses (127.0.0.0/8) are unusual routing targets.
match-value-warning.exact-ip-multicast: Multicast addresses (224.0.0.0/4) are unusual routing targets.
match-value-warning.zone-compound: Compound zone (label.label) is accepted by the parser but unusual; consider a single-label zone.

behavior.label: When the rules file changes on disk

section-hint.zones: Zone-level group routing. Matches all traffic for a named zone (e.g. .ru, corp-internal). Highest priority tier.
section-hint.domains: Domain name rules. Exact FQDN (example.com) or subdomain wildcard (*.example.com). Exact match takes priority over wildcard.
section-hint.ip: Exact IPv4 address rules. One address per entry. CIDR and IPv6 are not supported yet.
section-hint.windows: Windows application rules matched by process filename — exact or glob (e.g. *vpn*.exe). Applied on Windows only.
section-hint.linux: Linux application rules matched by process name. Stored in the file on all platforms, but applied only on Linux.
section-hint.macos: macOS application rules matched by bundle ID or process name. Stored in the file on all platforms, but applied only on macOS.

pro-section.badge-tooltip: Rules in this section are kept in the file but not applied in this version.

suggestions.chip-description: Review addresses the service suggests adding to your rules.
suggestions.body: Without these addresses the sites you routed may not work fully. Checked ones will be added to your rules.

inbox.clear-all-body: {count} suggestions will be forgotten together with your answers, so they can be offered again if they turn up beside your sites. This cannot be undone.
inbox.title: Addresses your sites need
inbox.intro: These addresses were pulled in by sites you route. Adding one sends it through the additional route together with the site that needs it. Anything you leave alone keeps going through the main route.
inbox.empty: Nothing is waiting for an answer right now.
inbox.consumer-on-primary-hint: This site goes through the main route. If you move the address into the tunnel, this site's traffic to it goes there too.
inbox.consumer-copy-hint: Right-click to copy this name to the clipboard.
inbox.behavior-stalls: connections to it stall on the main route
inbox.search-placeholder: Search by domain, host, or site
inbox.select-all-tooltip: Select or clear every address currently shown.
inbox.action-forget-tooltip: Removes the record entirely, answer and all, so the address is offered again if it turns up next to your sites.

table.intro: Every address below was pulled in by a site you route. Adding one sends it through the additional route together with the site that needs it — anything you leave alone keeps going through the main route. A dismissed address only stops being offered; "Allow again" lifts that suppression and nothing else.

reason.blocked-by-rule: A rule blocks this address directly.

diagnostic-mode.warning-banner: Extended diagnostics are active. More detailed information is being logged.

cache.os-flush-failed: Could not flush the OS DNS cache.
cache.entries-search-placeholder: Exact name or IP; *.google.com — subdomains; *google* — any match
cache.entries-bridge-unavailable: Service bridge not connected — cache entries unavailable
cache.entries-redacted-notice: Hostnames and IPs are reduced for privacy. Enable Extended diagnostics for full detail.
cache.render-truncated: Showing the first %1 of %2 matches — refine your search to narrow it.

seed-browser-history.started: Import started — hosts matching your rules will appear in the cache.

cache.auto-seed-label: Seed the cache from browser history automatically at service start
cache.auto-seed-privacy-note: Only visited hostnames are read from local browser profiles — nothing is sent anywhere.

conn-trace.title: Connection trace
conn-trace.subtitle: Recently-observed outbound connections and which interface they actually left through (primary, or the additional adapter). Observation only — it never changes routing. Works on demand, no service restart needed; the list is kept in memory only. (Writing connections to the on-disk log stays an opt-in in Settings.) Shows TCP/UDP connections — a ping (ICMP) leaves no connection to observe, so a pinged address will not appear here.
conn-trace.entries-redacted-notice: Addresses are masked for privacy. Enable Extended diagnostics for full detail.
conn-trace.entries-bridge-unavailable: Service bridge not connected — connection trace unavailable
conn-trace.entries-no-match: No connections match the current filters
conn-trace.col-process-tip: The application that opened the connection. Hover a row's process name to see its full path.
conn-trace.col-remote-tip: The destination address and port the connection went to.
conn-trace.col-egress-tip: Which network link the connection actually left through: Primary (your main link), Additional (the VPN/secondary link), Loopback (local, never leaves the PC), Other (another adapter), Unknown (couldn't be determined). This is observation only — it never changes routing.
conn-trace.col-verdict-tip: Whether the connection was allowed or dropped. A "Blocked" row may be a Windows Firewall or antivirus drop — not necessarily NetRuleRouter.
conn-trace.show-local-tip: Connections to your own machine or your local network (loopback, link-local, private LAN addresses). They never leave your network, so they say nothing about routing.
conn-trace.leak-mismatch-tip: Mismatch: this address belongs to a rule routed to the additional adapter, but the connection was allowed out over the PRIMARY link — a leak indicator.
conn-trace.verdict-note: "Blocked" means the connection was dropped by a Windows filter — this can be Windows Firewall or your antivirus, not necessarily NetRuleRouter. NetRuleRouter never blocks traffic on your primary route.

enforcement.blocked-unknown-under-block-all: Note: “block all unresolved” is on and this name is not in the cache — while the additional adapter is unavailable this connection will be BLOCKED until the name is cached.

enforcement.collateral-smart-exempt: Some of this site's addresses are shared with sites routed via the additional adapter. Smart kill switch keeps them unblocked, so this site works — but routed traffic to those shared addresses is not leak-protected.
enforcement.collateral-risk-subdomain-rules: This name is not cached, but sites under the same domain are routed via the additional adapter. Large services often serve both from the same addresses, so a strict kill switch may block this site while the additional adapter is unavailable.

audit.clear-disabled-tooltip: The audit trail cannot be cleared by design. Use the Operational tab to clear runtime logs.

body.generic: You have unsaved changes. Continue anyway?

detail.rules-not-applied: The rules on screen have not been applied to the service yet.
detail.rules-not-saved: The rules on screen have not been saved to your rules file yet. The service is stopped, so the file is the only place they can be kept.

accessible.cancel: Cancel and stay on the current view

notifications.title: Notifications
notifications.dismiss-all-tooltip: Removes every notice that can be dismissed. Ones that mirror a live state stay until the state itself changes.

app-unresolved.title: App rules applied, but some apps weren't found
app-unresolved.body: NetRuleRouter couldn't find these programs (they may not be installed in a standard location, or aren't running), so their traffic isn't routed by your rules: {apps}. Launch the app, or check the program name in Rules.

strict-killswitch.title: Strict kill-switch is on
strict-killswitch.body: While the additional adapter (VPN) is down, ALL internet is blocked except your local network — including normal browsing — until it comes back. Switch to the best-effort variant in Settings → Routing behavior if you want your main connection to keep working when the VPN drops.

kill-switch-restored.title: Leak protection restored
kill-switch-restored.body: Leak protection was turned back on from your saved settings (the background service had been reset). If you didn't expect this, you can turn it off in Settings → Routing behavior.

update-available.title: A new version is available
update-available.body: NetRuleRouter {version} has been released (you are running {current}). Open the download page to update.

auto-rule-candidates.title: Addresses waiting to be added
auto-rule-candidates.body: The service found {count} addresses the sites you routed need.

reason.route-unavailable: The route this connection needed was unavailable.
reason.not-covered-by-rules: No rule covers this connection, so the default action blocked it.
reason.unattributed: NetRuleRouter blocked this connection, but could not identify which filter did it.
